title: A Simple Way To Attain Daily Improvement
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin shares a simple daily feedback ritual he developed to keep pushing his class toward continuous improvement, arguing that in classroom management there is no stasis — a class is either getting better or getting worse. The technique: draw a horizontal line on a sheet of paper, list three things the class is doing well above it and three things needing improvement below it, then share the list briefly (under a minute) each morning without lecturing, scolding, or excessive praise, simply stating what you liked and what you want fixed. He stresses the list should change daily based on observations made throughout the prior day, doesn't have to follow a strict three-and-three split, and will naturally narrow into smaller, more specific details over time as the class improves. The underlying claim is that students crave honest, direct feedback and rarely receive enough of it, and that consistent daily doses of it drive dramatic improvement within weeks when paired with the broader SCM approach.
points: Draw a line on paper: three things the class is doing well above, three things needing improvement below, and share it in under a minute every morning.
Deliver the feedback flatly, without lecturing, scolding, or excessive praise — it's information, not an emotional response.
The list should change daily based on what you noticed the previous day, and doesn't have to be a strict three-and-three split.
Over time the feedback should narrow from broad categories into smaller, more specific details as the class's baseline behavior improves.
Students crave honest, direct feedback and rarely get enough of it — a daily habit of giving it is what drives them to keep improving.
quotes: To be an effective teacher it’s critical to continually push your students to get better every day. There is no stasis.
Take out a sheet of paper and draw a horizontal line across the middle. On the top half, write three things your class is doing well.
You don’t have to go on and on about it. You won’t overly praise or do any lecturing or scolding. You’re simply giving feedback.
In other words, this is what I like and want to keep doing and this is what I don’t like and want to fix. It should take less than a minute.

In time, your list will no longer be so broad but will instead narrow in on smaller and smaller details. As long as you’re using the SCM approach, and striving for daily excellence, you’ll see dramatic improvement in just a few weeks.
Students don’t get enough of it. When they do, they naturally lean toward getting better.
